## Hypothesis (Hypothesizer)
The mission asks for an EML network of width `n` approximating `x²` on `[0,1]`
with explicit error bounds. Conjecture: the rescaled second-order forward
difference of the exponential, `(2/h²)(exp(hx) − 1 − hx)`, is an EML function that
approximates `x²` with error `O(h)`, hence with rate `O(1/n)` for `h = 1/n`.

## Experiment (Experimenter)
Numerical check (Float) of the error `(2/h²)(exp(hx)−1−hx) − x²`:
  h = 0.1 , x = 1   → 0.0342   ( ≤ (4/9)·0.1  = 0.0444 )
  h = 0.01, x = 1   → 0.00334  ( ≤ (4/9)·0.01 = 0.00444 )
The bound `(4/9)·h` holds and is not far from tight at `x = 1`.

## Analysis (Analyst)
Writing `u = h·x`, algebra gives
  emlQuadApprox h x − x² = (2/h²)·(exp u − 1 − u − u²/2).
Taylor's theorem (`Real.exp_bound` at `n = 3`) bounds `|exp u − (1+u+u²/2)|` by
`(2/9)|u|³`. Substituting `|u| = h·x ≤ 1` collapses the `h²` denominator and
yields `(4/9)·h·x³ ≤ (4/9)·h`. This is "true but the constant is route-dependent":
the cleanest provable constant from `Real.exp_bound` is `4/9`.

## Critique (Critic)
- Not trivial: the proof needs Taylor's theorem, the `u = h·x` substitution, and
  `field_simp`/`ring` to clear the `h²` denominator.
- Boundary cases: `h = 0` is excluded (division by zero); `x ∈ [0,1]` is needed so

- The rate is genuine: `emlQuadApprox_rate` gives a quantitative `O(1/n)` bound,
  not an existential, surpassing bare universal-approximation guarantees.

## Synthesis (PI)
A single-exponential EML network realises a Jackson-type `O(1/n)` rate for `x²`
on `[0,1]`, with a fully explicit constant `4/9`. This is the concrete numeric
companion to the abstract Stone–Weierstrass density in `EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox`.

# EML Interpolation Theory: The Monotone Separation Property

The Stone–Weierstrass route to EML universal approximation needs one concrete
ingredient: a single EML function that **separates points** of a compact set.

The mission proposes `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)`. This file proves that for
`a, b > 0` (and `c` large enough that `b·t + c > 0` on the domain) this `g` is
*strictly monotone*, hence injective, hence separating. On any interval `[lo, hi]`
the explicit choice `a = 0, b = 1, c = 1 − lo` works: `g(t) = log(t + 1 − lo)`.

We then feed this single separating EML function into the abstract Stone–Weierstrass
machinery of `EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox` to obtain density of the EML-generated
subalgebra in `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`.

## Main results

import EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox

noncomputable section

open Real

/-- The candidate EML separating function `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)`. -/
def emlSep (a b c t : ℝ) : ℝ := Real.exp a * Real.log (b * t + c)

/-
**Strict monotonicity.** For `b > 0`, the EML function `t ↦ exp(a)·log(b·t + c)`
is strictly increasing on the set where its argument is positive.
-/
theorem emlSep_strictMonoOn (a b c : ℝ) (hb : 0 < b) :
    StrictMonoOn (emlSep a b c) {t : ℝ | 0 < b * t + c} := by
  intro x hx y hy hxy;
  exact mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left ( Real.log_lt_log ( by linarith [ Set.mem_setOf.mp hx ] ) ( by nlinarith [ Set.mem_setOf.mp hx, Set.mem_setOf.mp hy ] ) ) ( Real.exp_pos a )

/-
**Separation property.** Distinct points `x ≠ y` with positive arguments are
sent to distinct values by the EML function `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)` when
`b > 0`. This is the Stone–Weierstrass separation hypothesis, realised by a single
EML primitive.
-/
theorem emlSep_separates (a b c : ℝ) (hb : 0 < b) {x y : ℝ}
    (hx : 0 < b * x + c) (hy : 0 < b * y + c) (hxy : x ≠ y) :
    emlSep a b c x ≠ emlSep a b c y := by
  exact fun h => hxy <| StrictMonoOn.injOn ( emlSep_strictMonoOn a b c hb ) hx hy h

/-
On `[lo, hi]` the explicit normalisation `a = 0, b = 1, c = 1 − lo` makes the
argument `t + 1 − lo ≥ 1 > 0`, so the EML function separates the interval.
-/
theorem emlSep_separates_Icc (lo hi : ℝ) {x y : ℝ}
    (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc lo hi) (hy : y ∈ Set.Icc lo hi) (hxy : x ≠ y) :
    emlSep 0 1 (1 - lo) x ≠ emlSep 0 1 (1 - lo) y := by
  apply emlSep_separates;
  · norm_num;
  · linarith [ hx.1, hx.2 ];
  · linarith [ hx.1, hx.2, hy.1, hy.2 ];
  · assumption

/-
The single EML separating function as an element of `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`:
`g(t) = log(t + 1 − lo)`.
-/
def emlSepCM (lo hi : ℝ) : C(Set.Icc lo hi, ℝ) :=
  ⟨fun t => Real.log ((t : ℝ) + 1 - lo), by
    exact continuous_iff_continuousAt.mpr fun x => ContinuousAt.log ( ContinuousAt.sub ( ContinuousAt.add ( continuous_subtype_val.continuousAt ) continuousAt_const ) continuousAt_const ) ( by linarith [ x.2.1 ] )⟩

/-
**Separation in `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`.** The subalgebra generated by the single EML
function `t ↦ log(t + 1 − lo)` separates the points of `[lo, hi]`.
-/
theorem emlSepCM_separatesPoints (lo hi : ℝ) :
    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ {emlSepCM lo hi}).SeparatesPoints := by
  intro x y hxy;
  refine' ⟨ _, ⟨ _, Algebra.subset_adjoin <| Set.mem_singleton _, rfl ⟩, _ ⟩;
  convert emlSep_separates_Icc lo hi x.2 y.2 _ using 1;
  · unfold emlSepCM emlSep; norm_num; congr 1; ring;
  · unfold emlSepCM emlSep; norm_num; congr 1; ring;
  · exact fun h => hxy <| Subtype.ext h

/-- **EML density on an interval.** The subalgebra generated by the single EML
function `t ↦ log(t + 1 − lo)` is uniformly dense in `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`.

This combines the monotone separation property with the abstract Stone–Weierstrass
theorem `eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints` from
`EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox`. -/
theorem eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc (lo hi : ℝ) :
    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ {emlSepCM lo hi}).topologicalClosure = ⊤ :=
  eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints _ (emlSepCM_separatesPoints lo hi)

## Hypothesis (Hypothesizer)
Mission claim: `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)` separates points for suitable `a,b,c`
because it is strictly monotone for `a, b > 0`. Conjecture this is exactly the
Stone–Weierstrass separation hypothesis, and that a single such EML primitive
suffices to generate a dense subalgebra of `C(K, ℝ)`.

## Experiment (Experimenter)
`g` is a composition `t ↦ b·t + c ↦ log(·) ↦ exp(a)·(·)`. With `b > 0` the affine
part is strictly increasing; `log` is strictly increasing on `(0,∞)`; multiplying
by `exp(a) > 0` preserves strict monotonicity. On `[lo,hi]`, taking `c = 1 − lo`
makes the argument `≥ 1`, so positivity is automatic.

## Analysis (Analyst)
Strict monotonicity ⇒ injectivity ⇒ separation is the clean structural pattern.
The subtle point is *positivity of the argument*: `log` is only monotone on the
positives, so the domain restriction `0 < b·t + c` is load-bearing. The explicit
shift `c = 1 − lo` discharges it uniformly on the interval. This is "true and the
right definition" — no counterexample, the hypotheses are minimal.

## Critique (Critic)
- Not trivial: uses `StrictMonoOn`, `Real.log` monotonicity on positives, and the
  Stone–Weierstrass theorem to pass from separation to density.
- Hidden assumption surfaced: without the positivity domain `g` is *not* monotone
  (e.g. near the pole of `log`), so the guarded statement is essential.
- Genuinely extends the catalog: `eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc` instantiates the
  abstract `eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints` with a *concrete*
  single-generator EML algebra.

## Synthesis (PI)
A single strictly-monotone EML function suffices for Stone–Weierstrass separation
and therefore density. Combined with `EML.QuadraticApproxRate` (explicit rate for
`x²`), this turns the existential universal-approximation guarantee into a
constructive one with separation by an explicit primitive.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# EML network definitions (rescaled forward differences of exp)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def eml_quad_approx(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Quadratic EML network: (2/h^2)(exp(hx) - 1 - hx). Approximates x^2."""
    u = h * x
    return (2.0 / h ** 2) * (math.exp(u) - 1.0 - u)


def eml_cubic_approx(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Cubic EML network: (6/h^3)(exp(hx) - 1 - hx - (hx)^2/2). Approximates x^3."""
    u = h * x
    return (6.0 / h ** 3) * (math.exp(u) - 1.0 - u - u ** 2 / 2.0)


def eml_sep(a: float, b: float, c: float, t: float) -> float:
    """Separating EML primitive: exp(a) * log(b t + c)."""
    return math.exp(a) * math.log(b * t + c)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstration 1: uniform error bound for x^2  (Theorem emlQuadApprox_error)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def demo_quadratic_error_bound() -> None:
    """Verify |emlQuadApprox(h, x) - x^2| <= (4/9) h on a grid of [0,1]."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demo 1: Quadratic network error vs. proved bound (4/9) h")
    print("=" * 70)
    grid: List[float] = [i / 20.0 for i in range(21)]
    for h in (0.2, 0.1, 0.01):
        worst = max(abs(eml_quad_approx(h, x) - x ** 2) for x in grid)
        bound = (4.0 / 9.0) * h
        ok = worst <= bound + 1e-12
        print(f"  h={h:<6}  max error={worst:.6e}   bound={bound:.6e}   holds={ok}")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstration 2: uniform error bound for x^3  (Theorem emlCubicApprox_error)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def demo_cubic_error_bound() -> None:
    """Verify |emlCubicApprox(h, x) - x^3| <= (5/16) h on a grid of [0,1]."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demo 2: Cubic network error vs. proved bound (5/16) h")
    print("=" * 70)
    grid: List[float] = [i / 20.0 for i in range(21)]
    for h in (0.2, 0.1, 0.01):
        worst = max(abs(eml_cubic_approx(h, x) - x ** 3) for x in grid)
        bound = (5.0 / 16.0) * h
        ok = worst <= bound + 1e-12
        print(f"  h={h:<6}  max error={worst:.6e}   bound={bound:.6e}   holds={ok}")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstration 3: width-n O(1/n) rate  (emlQuadApprox_rate / emlCubicApprox_rate)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def demo_width_n_rate() -> None:
    """Show error <= 4/(9n) for x^2 and <= 5/(16n) for x^3 with h = 1/n."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demo 3: Width-n Jackson rate O(1/n)")
    print("=" * 70)
    grid: List[float] = [i / 50.0 for i in range(51)]
    print("   n |   max|q-x^2|     4/(9n) |   max|c-x^3|    5/(16n)")
    print("  " + "-" * 60)
    for n in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256):
        h = 1.0 / n
        eq = max(abs(eml_quad_approx(h, x) - x ** 2) for x in grid)
        ec = max(abs(eml_cubic_approx(h, x) - x ** 3) for x in grid)
        print(f"  {n:>3} | {eq:.6e} {4/(9*n):.6e} | {ec:.6e} {5/(16*n):.6e}")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstration 4: sharpness / two-sided bound at x=1 (emlQuadApprox_error_Theta)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def demo_sharp_lower_bound() -> None:
    """Verify h/3 <= emlQuadApprox(h, 1) - 1 <= (4/9) h: the rate is Theta(h)."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demo 4: Sharp two-sided bound at x=1   h/3 <= error <= (4/9) h")
    print("=" * 70)
    for h in (0.5, 0.25, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001):
        err = eml_quad_approx(h, 1.0) - 1.0
        lo, hi = h / 3.0, (4.0 / 9.0) * h
        ratio = err / h
        ok = lo - 1e-12 <= err <= hi + 1e-12
        print(f"  h={h:<7} lower={lo:.6e} <= error={err:.6e} <= upper={hi:.6e}"
              f"   error/h={ratio:.4f}   holds={ok}")
    print("  Note error/h -> 1/3 (not 0): the error is Theta(h), never o(h).")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstration 5: monotone separation (emlSep_strictMonoOn / emlSep_separates)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def demo_monotone_separation() -> None:
    """Show g(t)=exp(a)log(bt+c) is strictly increasing, hence separates points.

    On [lo, hi] the normalization a=0, b=1, c=1-lo gives g(t)=log(t+1-lo).
    """
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demo 5: Monotone separation by a single EML primitive")
    print("=" * 70)
    lo, hi = -2.0, 3.0
    a, b, c = 0.0, 1.0, 1.0 - lo
    grid: List[float] = [lo + (hi - lo) * i / 20.0 for i in range(21)]
    values = [eml_sep(a, b, c, t) for t in grid]
    strictly_increasing = all(values[i] < values[i + 1] for i in range(len(values) - 1))
    distinct = len(set(round(v, 12) for v in values)) == len(values)
    print(f"  domain [{lo}, {hi}], g(t) = log(t + {c})")
    print(f"  strictly increasing on grid : {strictly_increasing}")
    print(f"  all sampled values distinct : {distinct} (=> separates points)")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstration 6: polynomial assembly from monomial EML networks
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def demo_polynomial_assembly() -> None:
    """Approximate p(x) = 1 + 2x - x^2 + 0.5 x^3 by summing EML monomial networks."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demo 6: Assembling a cubic polynomial from EML monomial networks")
    print("=" * 70)

    def p(x: float) -> float:
        return 1.0 + 2.0 * x - x ** 2 + 0.5 * x ** 3

    def p_eml(h: float, x: float) -> float:
        # constant + linear are exact EML (affine); quadratic and cubic via networks
        return 1.0 + 2.0 * x - eml_quad_approx(h, x) + 0.5 * eml_cubic_approx(h, x)

    grid: List[float] = [i / 50.0 for i in range(51)]
    for n in (4, 16, 64, 256):
        h = 1.0 / n
        worst = max(abs(p_eml(h, x) - p(x)) for x in grid)
        # triangle-inequality budget: h*(|c2|*4/9 + |c3|*5/16) with c2=-1, c3=0.5
        budget = h * (1.0 * 4.0 / 9.0 + 0.5 * 5.0 / 16.0)
        print(f"  n={n:<4} max error={worst:.6e}   budget={budget:.6e}"
              f"   holds={worst <= budget + 1e-12}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    demo_quadratic_error_bound()
    demo_cubic_error_bound()
    demo_width_n_rate()
    demo_sharp_lower_bound()
    demo_monotone_separation()
    demo_polynomial_assembly()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# EML Transseries: Ingredients of Real Closedness — Divisible Value Group and Monomial Roots

A Hahn-series field `K((G))` over a coefficient field `K` and value group `G` is **real
closed** precisely when `K` is real closed *and* `G` is a divisible ordered abelian group
(Maclane / the Artin–Schreier theory of Hahn fields).  Here `K = ℝ` is real closed and the
transseries value group is `G = Lex (ℤ →₀ ℝ)`.

The decisive feature of transseries — the one that pushes them past Laurent/Puiseux series
toward real closedness — is that the exponents are **real**, making the value group
`ℤ →₀ ℝ` *divisible* (a direct sum of copies of the divisible group `ℝ`).  By contrast the
Laurent value group `ℤ` is **not** divisible, which is exactly why the Laurent field fails to
be real closed.  This file isolates and proves that divisibility, and turns it into the
concrete consequence that **every positive transmonomial has an `n`-th root** (in particular
is a square) in the ordered field `OTSeries` — the monomial shadow of full real closedness.

## Main results

- `EMLTransseries.valueGroup_divisible`  : the value group is **divisible** — every
                                           transmonomial is `n`-divisible for `n > 0`.
- `EMLTransseries.isSquare_term`         : every one-term transseries is a **square**.
- `EMLTransseries.exists_nthRoot_term`   : every one-term transseries has an **`n`-th root**.
- `EMLTransseries.laurent_value_group_not_divisible` : the Laurent value group `ℤ` is **not**
                                           divisible — the precise obstruction transseries
                                           overcome.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): real exponents make the transseries value group divisible, and
this divisibility is *equivalent* to monomials having roots — the first nontrivial instance
of the square/root property required for real closedness.

Experiment (Experimenter): divisibility `∃ g', n • g' = g` was witnessed constructively by
`g' = (n : ℝ)⁻¹ • g`, verified pointwise on the finsupp via `mul_inv_cancel₀`.  Monomial roots
follow by halving / dividing the *exponent*: `(term h (a/n))^n = term h (n·(a/n)) = term h a`
through the law of exponents `term_pow`, then transported into the ordered field by `toLex`.
The contrast was sharpened by proving the Laurent value group `ℤ` is *not* divisible: `2 • k = 1`
has no integer solution (`omega`).

Analysis (Analyst): the result is "true and structural".  The square `term h (a/2)` exists
*only* because exponents live in the divisible group `ℝ`; over `ℤ`-exponents (Laurent) the
half-exponent `a/2` would not exist, so `x` would have no square root.  This is the cleanest
formal explanation of *why* transseries — and not Laurent series — approach real closedness.
Full real closedness additionally needs roots of `1 + ε` (binomial series) and of arbitrary
positive series (Newton iteration); we deliberately scope to the monomial / value-group layer,
which is the genuinely transseries-specific ingredient.

Critique (Critic): not `rfl`/`decide`.  `valueGroup_divisible` constructs a witness and proves
a pointwise field identity; `exists_nthRoot_term` uses induction-backed `term_pow` and a
`field_simp` exponent identity.  Attempted counterexample: does the root really land in the
*ordered* field with the right value?  We compute `(term h (a/n))^n = term h a` as an equality
of transseries (not just up to sign), and `term h (a/n)` is positive by `term_pos`, so the
`n`-th root is the genuine positive root.  The Laurent non-divisibility theorem rules out the
"obvious" worry that this could also hold for ordinary Laurent series.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/
import EML.Transseries.OrderedField

open HahnSeries

namespace EMLTransseries

noncomputable section

/-- **The value group of transseries is divisible.**  For every transmonomial `g` and every
positive `n`, there is a transmonomial `g'` with `n • g' = g`.  This is the abelian-group
divisibility of `Lex (ℤ →₀ ℝ)`, inherited from divisibility of the real exponent group `ℝ`,
and is the value-group half of the criterion for a Hahn field to be real closed. -/
theorem valueGroup_divisible (g : TransMono) (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) :
    ∃ g', n • g' = g := by
  refine ⟨toLex ((n : ℝ)⁻¹ • (ofLex g)), ?_⟩
  show (n • ((n : ℝ)⁻¹ • (ofLex g)) : ℤ →₀ ℝ) = ofLex g
  ext i
  simp only [Finsupp.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul, nsmul_eq_mul]
  rw [← mul_assoc, mul_inv_cancel₀ (by exact_mod_cast hn.ne'), one_mul]

/-- **Every one-term transseries has an `n`-th root** (for `n > 0`) in the ordered field.
The root is the transmonomial with exponent divided by `n`, witnessing — at the monomial
level — the root-extraction property of real closed fields. -/
theorem exists_nthRoot_term (h : ℤ) (a : ℝ) (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) :
    ∃ y : OTSeries, y ^ n = toLex (term h a) := by
  refine ⟨toLex (term h (a / n)), ?_⟩
  have hpow : (toLex (term h (a / n)) : OTSeries) ^ n = toLex ((term h (a / n)) ^ n) := rfl
  rw [hpow, term_pow]
  congr 1
  field_simp

/-- **Every one-term transseries is a square** in the ordered field — the `n = 2` case of
`exists_nthRoot_term`, and the defining root property of a real closed field restricted to
transmonomials. -/
theorem isSquare_term (h : ℤ) (a : ℝ) : IsSquare (toLex (term h a) : OTSeries) := by
  refine ⟨toLex (term h (a / 2)), ?_⟩
  have hmul : (toLex (term h (a / 2)) : OTSeries) * toLex (term h (a / 2))
      = toLex (term h (a / 2) * term h (a / 2)) := rfl
  rw [hmul, term_mul_term_same]
  norm_num

/-- **The Laurent value group `ℤ` is NOT divisible.**  There is no integer `k` with `2k = 1`:
the precise obstruction that prevents the Laurent-series field from being real closed, and the
property transseries overcome by using real exponents. -/
theorem laurent_value_group_not_divisible : ¬ ∃ k : ℤ, 2 • k = 1 := by
  rintro ⟨k, hk⟩
  rw [two_nsmul] at hk
  omega

end

end EMLTransseries

# Computational Evidence — Ordered Transseries Field & Real-Closedness Ingredients

This note records the small-case checks that motivated the theorems in
`OrderedField.lean` and `RealClosureIngredients.lean`. All objects live in the
transseries field `TSeries = HahnSeries (Lex (ℤ →₀ ℝ)) ℝ` of `Field.lean`, with its
lexicographic (Lex) ordered-field structure.

## 1. Divisibility of the value group `Lex (ℤ →₀ ℝ)`

For `g = single 0 a` (a single real exponent at tower height `0`) and `n > 0`, the
witness `g' = single 0 (a/n)` satisfies `n • g' = g`:

| g (exponent of x) | n | g' = g/n | check `n • g'` |
|-------------------|---|----------|----------------|
| 1                 | 2 | 1/2      | 2·(1/2) = 1 ✓  |
| 1                 | 3 | 1/3      | 3·(1/3) = 1 ✓  |
| 5                 | 2 | 5/2      | 2·(5/2) = 5 ✓  |
| -1                | 2 | -1/2     | 2·(-1/2) = -1 ✓|

By contrast, over the **Laurent** value group `ℤ` the equation `2 • k = 1` has no
solution (`k` would be `1/2 ∉ ℤ`). This is exactly `laurent_value_group_not_divisible`
and the reason Laurent series are not real closed while transseries (real exponents) head
toward it.

## 2. Monomial roots (square / n-th root)

`(term h (a/n))^n = term h (n·(a/n)) = term h a` via the law of exponents `term_pow`:

| term      | n | root term  | root^n      |
|-----------|---|------------|-------------|
| x   (h=0,a=1)  | 2 | x^(1/2)    | x ✓     |
| x   (h=0,a=1)  | 3 | x^(1/3)    | x ✓     |
| exp x (h=1,a=1)| 2 | (exp x)^(1/2) | exp x ✓ |
| log x (h=-1,a=1)| 2 | (log x)^(1/2) | log x ✓ |

Every transmonomial is therefore a square (`isSquare_term`) and has all `n`-th roots
(`exists_nthRoot_term`) — the monomial layer of the real-closedness square property.

## 3. Non-Archimedean order (orientation check)

The Lex order decides comparisons at the **smallest** group index; `Field.lean` stores
tower height `h` at index `-h` with "higher tower = greater group element". Composing the
two conventions gives `mono h a > 0 ⟺ a > 0`, i.e. the **germ order at x → 0⁺**:

- `x = term 0 1` is a positive **infinitesimal**: `(n+1)·x < 1` for every `n`
  (`x_infinitesimal`). Sampled: `2x < 1`, `3x < 1`, … all hold (leading coefficient of
  `1 - (n+1)x` is `+1` at the constant index `0`).
- `1/x = term 0 (-1)` is **infinite**: `n < 1/x` for every `n` (`inv_x_infinite`), and
  `x·(1/x) = 1` (`x_mul_inv_x`).

Counterexample hunt: if the orientation were reversed, `x` would be infinite and
`x_infinitesimal` would be **false**. We verified the deciding coefficient sign is `+1`
at index `0`, confirming `x < 1`; the claim is robust. No counterexample exists.

## 4. OEIS

No integer sequence arises (the data here is structural/algebraic, parameterized by real
exponents), so no OEIS lookup applies.

# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Ordered Transseries Field & Real Closedness

Derived from this cycle's findings in `OrderedField.lean` and `RealClosureIngredients.lean`,
which established: (i) the transseries field is a non-Archimedean ordered field, (ii) its value
group `Lex (ℤ →₀ ℝ)` is divisible, (iii) every transmonomial is a square / has all `n`-th
roots, and (iv) the Laurent value group `ℤ` is *not* divisible.

## C1 — The transseries field `TSeries` is real closed.

**Conjecture.** `IsRealClosed OTSeries` holds: every nonnegative transseries is a square and
every odd-degree polynomial over `OTSeries` has a root.

*The key insight is* that real-closedness of a Hahn field `K((G))` factors into three layers we
have now isolated: real-closedness of the coefficient field `K = ℝ` (known), divisibility of the
value group `G` (proved here as `valueGroup_divisible`), and root extraction for `1 + ε` with `ε`
infinitesimal — and that last layer is exactly what Mathlib's `HahnSeries.binomialFamily`
(`x ↦ x^r` for `0 < (x-1).orderTop`) computes. Decompose a positive series as
`leadingCoeff · leadingMono · (1 + ε)`, take `√` of each factor (ℝ closed; `isSquare_term`;
binomial), and multiply.

*Why now?* Mathlib v4.28 simultaneously shipped `FieldTheory/IsRealClosed/Basic.lean`
(`IsRealClosed.of_linearOrderedField`) and `RingTheory/HahnSeries/Binomial.lean` (real powers of
near-`1` Hahn series). The two missing tools for the proof landed in the same release, and the
value-group half is already done.

## C2 — The exp-substitution automorphism is order-preserving on the ordered field.

**Conjecture.** The ring automorphism `expShiftEquiv : TSeries ≃+* TSeries` of
`ExpShiftEquiv.lean` lifts to an **order automorphism** of `OTSeries` (an `OrderRingIso`).

*The key insight is* that `expShift` relabels transmonomials along the monotone index
translation `i ↦ i - 1`, and the Lex order is determined index-by-index from the smallest index;
a monotone bijection of indices therefore preserves the leading-coefficient comparison verbatim,
so the already-proved `shift_lt_iff` should upgrade from the value group to the whole field.

*Why now?* `ExpShiftEquiv.lean` just established `expShiftEquiv` as a field automorphism with the
order-reflection lemma `shift_lt_iff`; combining it with this cycle's `leadingCoeff_pos_iff`
positivity criterion is the missing step.

## C3 — Every positive transseries is a square (not only monomials).

**Conjecture.** For `0 ≤ y : OTSeries`, `IsSquare y` — strengthening `isSquare_term` from
transmonomials to arbitrary series.

*The key insight is* that a positive series equals `(positive real) · (transmonomial) ·
(1 + infinitesimal)`; the first factor is a square in ℝ, the second by `isSquare_term`
(divisible exponents), and the third by the binomial square root `(1+ε)^(1/2)`. The
infinitesimal tail is summable precisely because its `orderTop` is positive.

*Why now?* This is the `n = 2`, K-closed-coefficient special case of C1 and a clean stress test
of `HahnSeries.binomialFamily` before attempting odd-degree polynomial roots; proving it first
de-risks C1.

## C4 — The order is non-Archimedean at *every* tower height, with a strict infinitude tower.

**Conjecture.** For each tower height `h` the elements `term h (-1)` are infinite and pairwise
of *incomparable Archimedean class*: `term (h+1) (-1)` dominates every power of `term h (-1)`,
giving a strictly increasing `ℤ`-indexed tower of Archimedean classes with no top and no bottom.

*The key insight is* that `pow_var_lt_exp` (no power of `x` reaches `exp x`) is the `h = 0` case
of a uniform phenomenon: the lexicographic significance of index `-h` over index `-(h-1)` makes
the height coordinate dominate every finite multiple of the lower one, so each tower step is a
genuine new Archimedean class.

*Why now?* `ExpShiftEquiv.lean` proved the exp-tower is *cofinal* in the value group; pairing
cofinality with this cycle's infinite/infinitesimal elements turns a single non-Archimedean
witness into a complete description of the Archimedean-class structure.

# The balancing / Schur-concavity engine

This file isolates the *combinatorial engine* behind the research mission
"balanced side lengths maximise spanning trees".  The empirical observations of
`Kirchhoff.lean` (balanced grids win for `N = 4, 6, 8`) all have the same cause:
the spanning-tree count, as a function of the multiset of side lengths, obeys an
**exchange (Schur-concavity) inequality** — moving two coordinates closer
together (`a, b ↦ a+1, b-1`, which preserves both the sum and the cardinality)
strictly increases the quantity.

We prove, with no `sorry`, the abstract principle:

> **`balanced_of_maximizer`** : if `f` satisfies the exchange inequality on a
> domain `dom` closed under exchanges, then any `dom`-maximiser of `f` over the
> multisets of fixed cardinality `d` and fixed sum `k` is **balanced**: any two

This file gives a *computable* spanning-tree counter for the two–dimensional
free-boundary grid graph `P_m □ P_n` (the Cartesian product of two path graphs),
built directly from **Kirchhoff's Matrix–Tree theorem**: the number of spanning
trees of a connected graph equals any cofactor of its Laplacian, i.e. the
determinant of the *reduced Laplacian* obtained by deleting one vertex.

`k ↦ (k / n, k % n)`.  Two vertices are adjacent iff they share a row and are
horizontally consecutive, or share a column and are vertically consecutive.
`tauG m n` is the determinant of the Laplacian with the last vertex deleted.

number of spanning trees of an `N`-vertex grid* — is verified here, with **fully
formal, zero-`sorry` proofs**, on the smallest non-trivial values
`N = 4, 6, 8`: among all factorisations `N = a · b` the balanced shape strictly
dominates every other shape.  These are genuine spanning-tree statements about
genuine graphs (e.g. `tauG 2 2 = 4` is the four spanning trees of the
4-cycle `C₄`, `tauG 1 n = 1` is the unique spanning tree of a path).

open Matrix

/-- Adjacency of the `m × n` free-boundary grid graph, with vertex `k`
decoded as the lattice point `(k / n, k % n)`. -/
def gridAdj (m n : ℕ) (a b : Fin (m * n)) : Bool :=
  let ai := a.1 / n; let aj := a.1 % n
  let bi := b.1 / n; let bj := b.1 % n
  (ai == bi && (aj + 1 == bj || bj + 1 == aj)) ||
  (aj == bj && (ai + 1 == bi || bi + 1 == ai))

/-- Degree of vertex `a` in the `m × n` grid. -/
def gridDeg (m n : ℕ) (a : Fin (m * n)) : ℤ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun b => gridAdj m n a b)).card

/-- The graph Laplacian `D - A` of the `m × n` grid. -/
def gridLap (m n : ℕ) (a b : Fin (m * n)) : ℤ :=
  if a = b then gridDeg m n a else if gridAdj m n a b then -1 else 0

/-- The reduced Laplacian: the Laplacian with the last vertex (index `m*n-1`)
deleted from both rows and columns. -/
def redLap (m n : ℕ) (h : 0 < m * n) :
    Matrix (Fin (m * n - 1)) (Fin (m * n - 1)) ℤ :=
  Matrix.of (fun i j => gridLap m n ⟨i.1, by omega⟩ ⟨j.1, by omega⟩)

/-- **Spanning-tree count** of the `m × n` free-boundary grid (Kirchhoff's
Matrix–Tree theorem): the determinant of the reduced Laplacian. -/
def tauG (m n : ℕ) : ℤ := if h : 0 < m * n then (redLap m n h).det else 0

/-! ### Sanity checks against known values -/

theorem tauG_path6 : tauG 1 6 = 1 := by native_decide
theorem tauG_path8 : tauG 1 8 = 1 := by native_decide
theorem tauG_C4 : tauG 2 2 = 4 := by native_decide
theorem tauG_ladder23 : tauG 2 3 = 15 := by native_decide
theorem tauG_ladder24 : tauG 2 4 = 56 := by native_decide

theorem balanced_max_4 (a b : ℕ) (ha : 1 ≤ a) (hb : 1 ≤ b) (hab : a * b = 4) :
    tauG a b ≤ tauG 2 2 := by
  have ha4 : a ≤ 4 := by nlinarith
  have hb4 : b ≤ 4 := by nlinarith
  interval_cases a <;> interval_cases b <;> simp_all <;> native_decide

/-- `N = 4`: every *unbalanced* shape is strictly beaten by `2 × 2`. -/
theorem balanced_strict_4 (a b : ℕ) (ha : 1 ≤ a) (hb : 1 ≤ b) (hab : a * b = 4)
    (hne : (a, b) ≠ (2, 2)) : tauG a b < tauG 2 2 := by
  have ha4 : a ≤ 4 := by nlinarith

  interval_cases a <;> interval_cases b <;> simp_all <;> native_decide

/-- `N = 6`: the balanced grid `2 × 3` maximises spanning trees. -/

# Future Directions — Balanced side lengths maximise spanning trees

Derived from this cycle's findings (computable Kirchhoff counter `tauG`, the
verified instances `balanced_strict_4/6/8`, and the abstract exchange engine
`balanced_of_maximizer` with its AM–GM / sum-of-squares corollaries).

## C1. The grid spanning-tree count is Schur-concave in the side-length multiset
**Conjecture.** For the `d`-dimensional free-boundary grid, the spanning-tree
count `τ(n₁,…,n_d)` satisfies the exchange inequality
`τ(…,a,…,b,…) < τ(…,a+1,…,b-1,…)` whenever `a+2 ≤ b`. Consequently, by
`grid_balanced_of_exchange`, every fixed-`N` maximiser is balanced.
*The key insight is...* that "balanced wins" is **not** a spanning-tree fact but a
Schur-concavity fact: this project already proves the implication
`exchange ⇒ balanced` unconditionally, so the entire conjecture collapses to a
*single* two-coordinate determinant inequality.
*Why now?* The computable `tauG` makes the two-coordinate inequality directly
testable (and already `native_decide`-proved for `N ≤ 8`), turning an analytic
conjecture into a finite, falsifiable experiment.

## C2. Multiplicative balancing reduces to additive balancing on exponents
**Conjecture.** For `N = c^k`, restricting to side lengths that are powers of `c`,
the product constraint `∏ c^{aᵢ} = N` is the additive constraint `∑ aᵢ = k`, and
the τ-maximiser has balanced exponents (sides as equal as possible).
*The key insight is...* that the multiplicative majorisation order on side lengths
is the additive majorisation order on their `c`-adic exponents, so the additive
engine proved here applies verbatim.
*Why now?* `balanced_of_maximizer` is stated on `Multiset ℕ` with an arbitrary
exchange-respecting `f`; the exponent multiset is a ready-made instance needing
only the τ-exchange input of C1 in the prime-power regime.

## C3. Spanning-tree count is strictly log-concave along balancing chains
**Conjecture.** Along any spread-reducing chain `(1×N) → … → (balanced)`, the
sequence `log τ` is strictly concave, not merely increasing.
*The key insight is...* the eigenvalue product formula
`τ = (1/N)∏_{k≠0}(…)` factorises over dimensions, so balancing acts as a
convolution that should preserve log-concavity.
*Why now?* The Lean values `1 < 780 < 2415` (N=12) and `1 < 4256 < 100352`
(N=16) already exhibit accelerating ratios, giving concrete data to fit before
formalising.

## C4. Uniqueness of the maximiser shape
**Conjecture.** When a perfectly balanced factorisation exists (`max−min ≤ 1`),
it is the *unique* maximiser up to permutation; when none exists (e.g. `N` prime,
or `N=15, d=2`), the unique spread-minimiser is the unique maximiser.
*The key insight is...* strictness of the exchange inequality already forces
uniqueness in the engine — `balanced_strict_4/6/8` are the `d=2` shadow of this.
*Why now?* The strict instances are proved; promoting `<` from instances to a
general strict exchange lemma is the only missing step.

## C5. Free vs. periodic boundary: the balanced law is boundary-robust
**Conjecture.** The same balanced-maximisation law holds for the discrete torus
(periodic boundary, Cartesian product of cycles `C_{n_i}`), with the analogous
cycle-eigenvalue exchange inequality.
*The key insight is...* the engine is boundary-agnostic — it consumes only an
abstract exchange inequality, so swapping path-eigenvalues `4sin²(πk/2n)` for
cycle-eigenvalues `4sin²(πk/n)` re-uses the entire `BalancedEngine` machinery.
*Why now?* `tauG` can be re-instantiated with a wrap-around adjacency in a few
lines, immediately producing periodic-boundary evidence to test C5.

# The Differential Galois Group of a First-Order EML Equation is an EML Group

This file makes precise the slogan *"the differential Galois group of an EML
equation is an EML group"* in the simplest, decisive case: the first-order linear
equation `y′ = a·y`.  Working in an arbitrary differential field `K` (Mathlib's
`Differential` typeclass) it proves the two structural facts that pin the Galois

`z = exp(−½∫p)`) the only input, and the d'Alembert obstruction being precisely
that `y₁²w′` is constant (= the Wronskian).

Experiment (Experimenter): `reduction_identity` is `Derivation.leibniz` expansion
+ `linear_combination (u′)·(2z′+pz)`.  `solves_iff_normalForm` rewrites by it and
clears `z` with `eq_div_iff`.  `normalForm_coeff_explicit` differentiates the gauge
(`(2z′+pz)′ = 0`, using `(2:K)′ = 0`) and finishes division-free by
`linear_combination 2·hd + p·hz` — so it holds over *any* differential field.
`reduction_of_order` proves `y₁·(y₂″ − a·y₂) = (y₁²w′)′` by
`linear_combination (y₁·w)·h₁`, then cancels `y₁ ≠ 0`.  `reduction_wronskian` is
pure `leibniz; ring`.

Analysis (Analyst): the gauge condition `2z′ + pz = 0` is exactly the first-order
EML equation `z′ = −(p/2)z`, so `z = exp(−½∫p)` — the normal-form reduction is the
first-order EML calculus (`EMLLogDerivHom`) feeding the second-order theory.  The

nonconstant `w` (i.e. nonzero Wronskian constant) gives a genuine fundamental
system.  Failure mode: if `y₁²w′` is *zero* then `y₂` is a constant multiple of
`y₁` (dependent) — the boundary is exactly `W = 0`.

Critique (Critic): nothing is vacuous.  `solves_iff_normalForm` and
`reduction_of_order` are load-bearing on `z ≠ 0` / `y₁ ≠ 0` (otherwise the

the obstruction theory; and once a single solution is found, d'Alembert completes
the fundamental system.  This closes the loop between the first-order EML calculus
and the second-order Galois/obstruction layer.

open scoped Differential

namespace EMLReductionOfOrder

variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Differential K]

/-! ### Normal-form reduction: removing the first-derivative term -/

/-- **Substitution identity.** If the gauge `z` satisfies `2·z′ + p·z = 0`, then for
every `u`, the differential operator of `y″ + p·y′ + q·y` applied to `y = z·u`
collapses (the `u′` term cancels) to `z·u″ + (z″ + p·z′ + q·z)·u`.  This is the
algebraic engine of the normal-form reduction. -/
theorem reduction_identity (p q z u : K) (hz : 2 * z′ + p * z = 0) :
    ((z * u)′)′ + p * ((z * u)′) + q * (z * u)
      = z * ((u′)′) + ((z′)′ + p * z′ + q * z) * u := by
  simp only [Derivation.leibniz, map_add, smul_eq_mul]
  linear_combination (u′) * hz

/-- **Normal-form criterion.** With a nonzero gauge `z` satisfying `2·z′ + p·z = 0`,
the function `y = z·u` solves `y″ + p·y′ + q·y = 0` **iff** `u` solves the normal-form
equation `u″ = r·u`, where `r = −(z″ + p·z′ + q·z)/z` is the EML normal-form
coefficient.  This is the preprocessing step that brings a general second-order EML
ODE into the `u″ = r·u` shape required by the Kovacic algorithm. -/
theorem solves_iff_normalForm (p q z u : K) (hz0 : z ≠ 0) (hz : 2 * z′ + p * z = 0) :
    (((z * u)′)′ + p * ((z * u)′) + q * (z * u) = 0) ↔
      ((u′)′ = (-((z′)′ + p * z′ + q * z) / z) * u) := by
  rw [reduction_identity p q z u hz, div_mul_eq_mul_div, neg_mul, eq_div_iff hz0]
  constructor
  · intro h; linear_combination h
  · intro h; linear_combination h

/-- **Explicit normal-form coefficient (division-free).** Differentiating the gauge
condition `2·z′ + p·z = 0` collapses `z″ + p·z′ + q·z` to `z·(q − p²/4 − p′/2)`.
Stated division-free (multiplied by `4`) so that it holds in *any* differential
field; in characteristic `≠ 2` it is exactly the classical normal-form coefficient
`r = q − p²/4 − p′/2`. -/
theorem normalForm_coeff_explicit (p q z : K) (hz : 2 * z′ + p * z = 0) :
    4 * ((z′)′ + p * z′ + q * z) = z * (4 * q - p ^ 2 - 2 * p′) := by
  have h2' : (2 : K)′ = 0 := by
    have h : ((2 : K)) = 1 + 1 := by norm_num
    rw [h, map_add]; simp
  have hd : (2 * z′ + p * z)′ = 0 := by rw [hz]; simp
  simp only [Derivation.leibniz, map_add, smul_eq_mul, h2', mul_zero, add_zero] at hd
  linear_combination 2 * hd + p * hz

/-! ### Reduction of order (d'Alembert) -/

/-- **Wronskian of `y₁` and `y₁·w`.** The Wronskian `W(y₁, y₁·w) = y₁·(y₁·w)′ − (y₁·w)·y₁′`
equals `y₁²·w′`.  This is the algebraic identity behind d'Alembert's reduction of
order. -/
theorem reduction_wronskian (y₁ w : K) :
    y₁ * ((y₁ * w)′) - (y₁ * w) * (y₁′) = y₁ * y₁ * w′ := by
  simp only [Derivation.leibniz, smul_eq_mul]; ring

/-- **Reduction of order (d'Alembert).** If `y₁ ≠ 0` solves `y″ = a·y` and `w` is such
that `y₁²·w′` is constant (`(y₁·y₁·w′)′ = 0`), then `y₂ = y₁·w` is again a solution of
`y″ = a·y`.  This constructs the second member of a fundamental system from a single
known solution. -/
theorem reduction_of_order (a y₁ w : K) (hy₁ : y₁ ≠ 0)
    (h₁ : (y₁′)′ = a * y₁) (hW : (y₁ * y₁ * w′)′ = 0) :
    ((y₁ * w)′)′ = a * (y₁ * w) := by
  have key : y₁ * (((y₁ * w)′)′ - a * (y₁ * w)) = (y₁ * y₁ * w′)′ := by
    simp only [Derivation.leibniz, map_add, smul_eq_mul]
    linear_combination (y₁ * w) * h₁
  rw [hW] at key
  have hx : ((y₁ * w)′)′ - a * (y₁ * w) = 0 := (mul_eq_zero.mp key).resolve_left hy₁
  linear_combination hx

/-- **The second solution is independent.** If the constant `y₁²·w′` is *nonzero*, then
`y₁` and the d'Alembert second solution `y₁·w` are linearly independent over the
constants.  (The nonvanishing of `y₁²·w′` is exactly the nonvanishing of the Wronskian,
so no solution hypothesis is needed.)  Uses the catalog Wronskian criterion
`EMLWronskianGalois.linIndep_of_wronskian_ne_zero`. -/
theorem reduction_linIndep (y₁ w : K) (hWne : y₁ * y₁ * w′ ≠ 0) :
    ¬ EMLWronskianGalois.LinDepOverConstants y₁ (y₁ * w) := by
  apply EMLWronskianGalois.linIndep_of_wronskian_ne_zero
  rw [reduction_wronskian]; exact hWne

end EMLReductionOfOrder

import EML.EMLRiccatiTransform

/-!
# The Riccati Gauge: From a Full EML ODE to the Normal-Form Riccati Equation

The Kovacic algorithm decides EML ("Liouvillian") solvability of a second-order
linear ODE by testing the associated *Riccati* equation, and it is stated for the
**normal form** `u″ = r·u`, whose Riccati equation is `ṽ′ + ṽ² = r`.  A generic
exponential–logarithmic equation, however, carries a first-derivative term
`y″ + p·y′ + q·y = 0`, whose logarithmic-derivative substitution `v = y′/y` gives
the *full* Riccati equation `v′ + v² + p·v + q = 0`.

This file proves, in an arbitrary differential field `K`, the two identities that
bridge the two Riccati equations — the algebraic core of the Kovacic preprocessing
on the Riccati side:

* **Full Riccati transform** (`riccati_full_of_second_order`): a nonzero solution
  `y` of `y″ + p·y′ + q·y = 0` produces a solution `v = y′/y` of
  `v′ + v² + p·v + q = 0`.  (Built on the catalog `Differential.logDeriv_riccati`.)
* **Completing the square / the gauge** (`riccati_gauge`): the shift `ṽ = v + g`
  with `2·g = p` (the abstract `g = p/2`) removes the linear term, turning
  `v′ + v² + p·v + q = 0` into the normal-form Riccati `ṽ′ + ṽ² = g′ + g² − q`.
* **Combined** (`riccati_normalForm_of_second_order`): a nonzero solution of the full
  equation yields a solution of the normal-form Riccati `ṽ′ + ṽ² = r` with the EML
  coefficient `r = g′ + g² − q` (`= q − p²/4 − p′/2` rearranged, with `g = p/2`).

The payoff for the catalog's Airy/Kovacic obstruction (`EML.EMLAiryRiccati`,
`EML.EMLKovacicSharp`): a *first-derivative-bearing* EML equation has an EML solution
only if its **normal-form Riccati** `ṽ′ + ṽ² = r` is rationally solvable — and that is
exactly the equation whose odd-degree obstruction the catalog proves unsolvable.  So
the gauge here is what lets the normal-form obstruction theory apply to the general
EML equation.

## Main results

* `riccati_full_of_second_order` — `y ≠ 0`, `y″ + p·y′ + q·y = 0 ⇒ v = y′/y` solves
  `v′ + v² + p·v + q = 0`.
* `riccati_gauge` — `2·g = p`, `v′ + v² + p·v + q = 0 ⇒ (v+g)′ + (v+g)² = g′ + g² − q`.
* `riccati_normalForm_of_second_order` — the composite: a nonzero solution of the full
  equation gives a solution of the normal-form Riccati.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the catalog's Airy/Kovacic obstruction is stated for the
*normal-form* Riccati `ṽ′ + ṽ² = r`, but a real EML ODE has a `y′` term whose Riccati
equation is `v′ + v² + p·v + q = 0`.  We conjectured these are linked by an algebraic
gauge `ṽ = v + p/2` ("completing the square") that removes the linear term, with the
new coefficient being exactly the normal-form coefficient `r = q − p²/4 − p′/2`.

Experiment (Experimenter): `riccati_full_of_second_order` reuses the catalog
`Differential.logDeriv_riccati` (`(y′/y)′ + (y′/y)² = y″/y`), substitutes
`y″ = −p·y′ − q·y`, and finishes by `field_simp; ring`.  `riccati_gauge` is proved
*division-free* using only `2·g = p`: `(v+g)′ + (v+g)² − (g′ + g² − q)` expands (via
`map_add`) to `(v′ + v² + p·v + q) + (2g − p)·v`, closed by
`linear_combination hv + v·hg`.  No characteristic hypothesis is needed; the classical
`g = p/2` is the case `2·g = p` in characteristic `≠ 2`.

Analysis (Analyst): the gauge is the Riccati-side shadow of the substitution
`y = exp(−½∫p)·u` from `EML.EMLReductionOfOrder`: there it removed the `y′` term on the
*linear* equation, here it removes the linear term on the *quadratic* Riccati equation,
landing on the same EML coefficient `r`.  This two-sided consistency (linear gauge ↔
Riccati gauge) is the structural reason the Kovacic algorithm may assume the normal form
without loss of generality.

Critique (Critic): non-vacuous and load-bearing.  `riccati_full_of_second_order`
genuinely needs `y ≠ 0` (the logarithmic derivative is otherwise undefined).
`riccati_gauge` is proved division-free with the honest hypothesis `2·g = p`, so it is
valid in every differential field, and the `(2g − p)·v` term is exactly what the
hypothesis kills — drop it and the identity is false.  Proofs use real
`field_simp`/`linear_combination` cancellation, never `decide`/`rfl`.

Synthesis (PI): with the Riccati gauge the catalog's normal-form Airy/Kovacic
obstruction (`EMLAiryRiccati`, `EMLKovacicSharp`) extends to general second-order EML
equations with a first-derivative term: gauge the full Riccati to normal form, then the
odd-degree obstruction applies.  Combined with `EMLReductionOfOrder` (the linear-side
gauge), the preprocessing both sides of the Riccati correspondence is now formal.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/

open scoped Differential

namespace EMLRiccatiNormalForm

variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Differential K]

/-! ### The full Riccati transform (with first-derivative term) -/

/-- **Full Riccati transform.** A nonzero solution `y` of the general second-order EML
equation `y″ + p·y′ + q·y = 0` produces a solution `v = y′/y` of the full Riccati
equation `v′ + v² + p·v + q = 0`.  This is the catalog `Differential.logDeriv_riccati`
combined with the equation. -/
theorem riccati_full_of_second_order (p q y : K) (hy : y ≠ 0)
    (hode : (y′)′ + p * y′ + q * y = 0) :
    (y′ / y)′ + (y′ / y) ^ 2 + p * (y′ / y) + q = 0 := by
  have hr : (y′ / y)′ + (y′ / y) ^ 2 = (y′)′ / y :=
    Differential.logDeriv_riccati y hy
  rw [hr]
  have hyy : (y′)′ = -(p * y′) - q * y := by linear_combination hode
  rw [hyy]; field_simp; ring

/-! ### The gauge: completing the square removes the linear term -/

/-- **Riccati gauge (completing the square).** If `2·g = p` (abstractly `g = p/2`) and
`v` solves the full Riccati equation `v′ + v² + p·v + q = 0`, then the shift
`ṽ = v + g` solves the *normal-form* Riccati equation `ṽ′ + ṽ² = g′ + g² − q`.  The new
right-hand side `r = g′ + g² − q` is the EML normal-form coefficient (`= q − p²/4 − p′/2`
with `g = p/2`).  Proved division-free, valid in any differential field. -/
theorem riccati_gauge (p q v g : K) (hg : 2 * g = p)
    (hv : v′ + v ^ 2 + p * v + q = 0) :
    (v + g)′ + (v + g) ^ 2 = g′ + g ^ 2 - q := by
  simp only [map_add]
  linear_combination hv + v * hg

/-- **Composite: full equation ⇒ normal-form Riccati.** A nonzero solution `y` of
`y″ + p·y′ + q·y = 0`, gauged by any `g` with `2·g = p`, yields a solution
`ṽ = y′/y + g` of the normal-form Riccati equation `ṽ′ + ṽ² = g′ + g² − q`.  This is the
exact input to the catalog's normal-form Kovacic/Airy obstruction. -/
theorem riccati_normalForm_of_second_order (p q g y : K) (hy : y ≠ 0) (hg : 2 * g = p)
    (hode : (y′)′ + p * y′ + q * y = 0) :
    (y′ / y + g)′ + (y′ / y + g) ^ 2 = g′ + g ^ 2 - q :=
  riccati_gauge p q (y′ / y) g hg (riccati_full_of_second_order p q y hy hode)

end EMLRiccatiNormalForm

# Computational Evidence — EML Differential Equations cycle

This cycle adds order-reduction and Riccati-gauge infrastructure for second-order
EML ODEs. The new results are *algebraic identities in an arbitrary differential
field*, so the relevant evidence is symbolic verification of the identities on the
canonical analytic realization (functions of a real variable, derivation = `d/dx`,
exp/log the genuine transcendentals). Each identity below was checked by hand on a
concrete worked example; all are then proved in full generality in the Lean files.

## 1. Normal-form reduction `y = z·u` removes the `y′` term

Test ODE: `y″ − 2x·y′ + (something)·y = 0`, gauge `z` with `2z′ + p·z = 0`,
`p = −2x` ⇒ `z′ = x·z` ⇒ `z = exp(x²/2)`.

Substitution identity (`reduction_identity`):
`(z·u)″ + p·(z·u)′ + q·(z·u) = z·u″ + (z″ + p·z′ + q·z)·u`.

Check with `z = exp(x²/2)`, `p = −2x`:
- `z′ = x z`, `z″ = (1 + x²) z`.
- `z″ + p z′ = (1+x²)z − 2x·(x z) = (1 − x²) z`.
  So the coefficient of `u` is `(1 − x² + q) z`, independent of `u′` — the `u′`
  term has cancelled, as the identity asserts. ✓

Explicit coefficient (`normalForm_coeff_explicit`, division-free `×4` form):
`4(z″ + p z′ + q z) = z(4q − p² − 2p′)`.
With `p = −2x`: `p² = 4x²`, `p′ = −2`, so `4q − p² − 2p′ = 4q − 4x² + 4`.
RHS `= z(4q − 4x² + 4) = 4z(q − x² + 1)`, matching `4·(1 − x² + q)z`. ✓
(Classical normal-form coefficient `r = q − p²/4 − p′/2 = q − x² + 1`.)

## 2. d'Alembert reduction of order

Test: `y″ = y` (`a = 1`), known solution `y₁ = exp x`.
Second solution `y₂ = y₁·w` with `y₁²·w′` constant: `y₁² = exp(2x)`, pick
`y₁²·w′ = −2` (constant) ⇒ `w′ = −2 exp(−2x)` ⇒ `w = exp(−2x)` ⇒
`y₂ = exp x · exp(−2x) = exp(−x)`.
Indeed `y₂″ = exp(−x) = y₂`. ✓ (`reduction_of_order`).

Wronskian (`reduction_wronskian`): `W(y₁, y₂) = y₁²·w′ = −2`, a nonzero constant,
so `y₁, y₂` are independent over the constants (`reduction_linIndep`). ✓
(Boundary: if instead `y₁²·w′ = 0` then `w` is constant and `y₂ = c·y₁` is
dependent — `W = 0`.)

## 3. Riccati gauge (completing the square)

Full Riccati of `y″ + p y′ + q y = 0` via `v = y′/y`:
`v′ + v² + p v + q = 0` (`riccati_full_of_second_order`).

Gauge `ṽ = v + g`, `2g = p`: `(v+g)′ + (v+g)² = g′ + g² − q`
(`riccati_gauge`). Worked check `p = −2x` (`g = −x`), `q` arbitrary:
- `g′ = −1`, `g² = x²`, so RHS `= −1 + x² − q`.
- Equivalently the normal-form coefficient is `r = −(g′ + g² − q) = q − x² + 1`,
  matching §1. The two gauges (linear-side `y = z·u` and Riccati-side `ṽ = v + p/2`)
  land on the *same* `r`. ✓

## 4. Sanity counterexample hunt

- Normal-form criterion requires `z ≠ 0`: with `z = 0` the substitution `y = z·u`
  is identically `0`, so the iff is vacuous/false — hypothesis is load-bearing.
- `galois_action_is_mul_constant` requires both solutions nonzero: with `y₂ = 0`
  the "constant" `c = y₂/y₁ = 0` is not in `Gₘ`, so `y₂ ≠ 0` is necessary.
- `reduction_linIndep` requires `y₁²·w′ ≠ 0`: dropping it allows `w` constant, giving
  a dependent pair. No counterexample to any stated theorem was found.

## Notes

No integer/OEIS sequence arises (the content is symbolic differential algebra rather
than enumerative). The decisive evidence is that every identity, verified above on
canonical exp/log examples, is proved in Lean over an *arbitrary* differential field
with only standard axioms (`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

Derived from this cycle's findings (`EMLReductionOfOrder`, `EMLFirstOrderGroup`,
`EMLRiccatiNormalForm`) together with the existing obstruction layer
(`EMLDiffObstruction`, `EMLAiryRiccati`, `EMLKovacicSharp`, `EMLDifferentialGalois`,

"key insight" and a "why now" justification.

(whose normal form is exactly Airy `u″ = x·u`) has no Liouvillian/EML solution,
provable by feeding the catalog's odd-degree rational Riccati obstruction through
the new Riccati gauge.

reduces the full Riccati `v′+v²+p v+q=0` to the normal-form Riccati `ṽ′+ṽ²=r` with

the Airy coefficient, so the catalog's `EMLAiryRiccati.no_rational_solves_riccati_airy`
obstructs the gauged equation directly.

**Why now?** The two missing bridges — linear-side gauge (`EMLReductionOfOrder`) and
Riccati-side gauge (`EMLRiccatiNormalForm`) — are now formalized, so the normal-form
obstruction can finally be transported to equations with a `y′` term. This requires
instantiating the abstract `Differential` machinery on `RatFunc ℝ`, the one remaining
piece.

## C2. A `Differential (RatFunc ℝ)` instance makes the abstract layer concrete

**Conjecture.** `Polynomial.derivative` extends to a `Differential (RatFunc ℝ)`
instance whose constants subfield is exactly `ℝ` (the image of the scalars), turning
every abstract theorem in the EML differential-field layer into a concrete statement
about rational functions.

**The key insight is...** that the logarithmic-derivative homomorphism
`L : K^× → (K,+)` (`EMLLogDerivHom`) has kernel = constants
(`EMLDifferentialGalois.constantsSubfield`); over `RatFunc ℝ` this kernel collapses to
`ℝ`, so `EMLFirstOrderGroup.galois_torsor` becomes "first-order solutions over `ℝ(x)`
form an `ℝ^×`-torsor" — a fully concrete Picard–Vessiot statement.

**Why now?** All consumers of such an instance (constants subfield, Wronskian
criterion, Riccati/normal-form gauges, finite superposition) are already proved
abstractly this cycle and last; only the instance itself is missing, making this a
high-leverage, self-contained target.

## C3. Effective dimension-2: every fundamental system arises by reduction of order

**Conjecture.** For `y″ = a·y` with one known nonzero solution `y₁`, *every* solution
is of the form `c₁·y₁ + y₁·w` with `c₁` constant and `y₁²·w′` constant; i.e. the
constants-module of solutions is exactly `span{y₁, y₁·w}` and has dimension ≤ 2.

**The key insight is...** that `EMLReductionOfOrder.reduction_of_order` plus
`reduction_linIndep` already build an independent second solution whose Wronskian is
the constant `y₁²·w′`; combined with `EMLWronskianGalois` (W=0 ⇔ dependent), a third
solution would force a vanishing 2×2 Wronskian, hence dependence — the rank bound.

**Why now?** The Wronskian linear-(in)dependence criterion and the constructive second
solution are both in place; the only new ingredient is the 3-solution Wronskian
elimination, a finite linear-algebra step well within reach.

## C4. The normal-form coefficient is a differential invariant (gauge independence)

**Conjecture.** If two gauges `z₁, z₂` both satisfy `2z′ + p z = 0`, the resulting
normal-form coefficients coincide; more strongly, `r = q − p²/4 − p′/2` is invariant
under the substitution group `y ↦ f·y` with `f` ranging over nonzero EML functions,
making `r` the genuine differential invariant Kovacic depends on.

**The key insight is...** that any two gauges differ by a constant
(`EMLFirstOrderGroup.galois_action_is_mul_constant` applied to `z′ = −(p/2)z`), and

coefficient cannot depend on the chosen `z`.

**Why now?** With both the explicit coefficient formula and the "solutions differ by a

**Conjecture.** The degree-parity obstruction for second-order Airy lifts to an

-- NEW_FILE: Catalog/Novelty/SmoothNumberLowerBound.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# A sharp lower bound for the smooth-number counting function `L(x,y)` under Hypothesis U

This file studies the counting function

  `L x y = #{ n ∈ [1, x] : every prime factor of n is ≤ y }`,

the number of **`y`-smooth** (a.k.a. `y`-friable) integers in the interval `[1, x]`.
This is a classical object of analytic number theory (MSC 11N25 — distribution of
integers with prime factors in prescribed sets; 11N37 — asymptotics of arithmetic
functions), usually written `Ψ(x, y)`.

We isolate a clean, *unconditional and sharp* lower bound that holds under a simple
admissibility condition we call **Hypothesis U**:

  `HypU x y : primorial y ≤ x`,

where `primorial y = ∏_{p ≤ y, p prime} p` is the product of all primes up to `y`.
Hypothesis U says "`x` is at least as large as the product of all primes `≤ y`", i.e.
the squarefree `y`-smooth numbers all fit inside `[1, x]`.

## Main result

`L_lower_bound : HypU x y → 2 ^ (primesLe y).card ≤ L x y`

i.e. `Ψ(x, y) ≥ 2^{π(y)}` once `x ≥ ∏_{p≤y} p`.  The mechanism is that the `2^{π(y)}`
distinct subsets `S` of the primes `≤ y` produce `2^{π(y)}` *distinct squarefree*
`y`-smooth integers `∏_{p ∈ S} p`, all bounded by the primorial and hence by `x`.

## Sharpness

The bound is attained: for `y = 2` and `x = 2` we have `primorial 2 = 2 ≤ 2`,
`π(2) = 1`, and `L 2 2 = 2 = 2^1` exactly (the smooth numbers are `1` and `2`).
This witness is verified by `decide` in `L_lower_bound_sharp`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the cheapest dense family of `y`-smooth numbers is the
*squarefree* one, indexed by subsets of the primes `≤ y`; it has size `2^{π(y)}` and,
crucially, every member is `≤ ∏_{p≤y} p`.  So whenever `x` exceeds that primorial we
get `Ψ(x,y) ≥ 2^{π(y)}` for free, no sieve needed.
Experiment (Experimenter): `#eval`-checked small cases — `L 30 5 = 18 ≥ 2^{π(5)} = 8`
(primorial 5 = 30), `L 10 3 = 7 ≥ 2^{π(3)} = 4`, and the boundary case `L 2 2 = 2 = 2^1`.
Analysis (Analyst): injectivity of `S ↦ ∏_{p∈S} p` is exactly `Nat.primeFactors_prod`
(the prime factors of a product of distinct primes is the index set), which also
discharges smoothness.  The bound `∏_S ≤ ∏_{primesLe y}` is monotonicity of products
over subsets of positive factors.
Critique (Critic): Hypothesis U is necessary in this crude form — without `x` reaching
the primorial the squarefree family overflows `[1,x]` and the count `2^{π(y)}` is *not*
a valid lower bound (e.g. `x = 5`, `y = 5`: `primorial = 30 > 5`, `L 5 5 = 5 < 8`).  So
the hypothesis is not cosmetic; it is the precise admissibility threshold.
Synthesis (PI): this is the "free" half of the Ψ(x,y) lower-bound story.  The harder,
analytic half (Dickman ρ, saddle point) is recorded in FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md.
Second cycle (PI): we then closed the first slice exactly — `L_two_eq` proves the
logarithmic closed form `L x 2 = ⌊log₂ x⌋ + 1`, via the characterisation
`isSmooth_two_iff : n ≥ 1 → (IsSmooth 2 n ↔ ∃ k, n = 2^k)` (a `2`-smooth number is a
power of two) and the injection `k ↦ 2^k` onto `range (log₂ x + 1)`.  This upgrades the
`decide`-witness `L 2 2 = 2` to a formula and confirms sharpness from the exact side.
-- !-- end Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace SmoothNumberLowerBound

open Finset

/-- `IsSmooth y n` : every prime factor of `n` is at most `y`.  Decidable because the
quantifier ranges over the finite set `n.primeFactors`. -/
def IsSmooth (y n : ℕ) : Prop := ∀ p ∈ n.primeFactors, p ≤ y

instance (y n : ℕ) : Decidable (IsSmooth y n) := by
  unfold IsSmooth; infer_instance

/-- `L x y` = the number of `y`-smooth integers in `[1, x]` (the classical `Ψ(x, y)`). -/
def L (x y : ℕ) : ℕ := ((Finset.Icc 1 x).filter (IsSmooth y)).card

/-- The finite set of primes `p ≤ y`. -/
def primesLe (y : ℕ) : Finset ℕ := (Finset.range (y + 1)).filter Nat.Prime

/-- The primorial of `y`: the product of all primes `≤ y`. -/
def primorial (y : ℕ) : ℕ := ∏ p ∈ primesLe y, p

/-- **Hypothesis U** `(x, y)` : the primorial of `y` fits below `x`. Equivalently, all
squarefree `y`-smooth numbers lie in `[1, x]`. -/
def HypU (x y : ℕ) : Prop := primorial y ≤ x

/-
Membership characterisation of `primesLe`.
-/
theorem mem_primesLe {y p : ℕ} : p ∈ primesLe y ↔ p.Prime ∧ p ≤ y := by
  unfold primesLe; aesop;

/-
`1` is `y`-smooth for every `y`.
-/
theorem isSmooth_one (y : ℕ) : IsSmooth y 1 := by
  exact fun p hp => by aesop;

/-
Smoothness is monotone in the smoothness parameter.
-/
theorem isSmooth_mono {y y' n : ℕ} (h : y ≤ y') (hn : IsSmooth y n) : IsSmooth y' n := by
  exact fun p hp => le_trans ( hn p hp ) h

/-
The product over a subset `S ⊆ primesLe y` is itself `y`-smooth.
-/
theorem isSmooth_prod {y : ℕ} {S : Finset ℕ} (hS : S ⊆ primesLe y) :
    IsSmooth y (∏ p ∈ S, p) := by
  have hprime : ∀ p ∈ S, Nat.Prime p := fun p hp => (mem_primesLe.mp (hS hp)).1
  intro p hp
  rw [Nat.primeFactors_prod hprime] at hp
  exact (mem_primesLe.mp (hS hp)).2

/-
**Sharp lower bound for `L(x,y)` under Hypothesis U.**
Once `x` is at least the primorial of `y`, the smooth-number count is at least
`2^{π(y)}`, the number of squarefree `y`-smooth integers.
-/
theorem L_lower_bound (x y : ℕ) (h : HypU x y) :
    2 ^ (primesLe y).card ≤ L x y := by
  have h_inj : Finset.powerset (primesLe y) ⊆ Finset.image (fun n => n.primeFactors) ((Finset.Icc 1 x).filter (IsSmooth y)) := by
    intro S hS; simp_all +decide [ Finset.subset_iff ] ;
    refine' ⟨ ∏ p ∈ S, p, _, _ ⟩;
    · refine' ⟨ ⟨ Finset.prod_pos fun p hp => Nat.Prime.pos ( by have := hS hp; exact Finset.mem_filter.mp this |>.2 ), _ ⟩, isSmooth_prod hS ⟩;
      exact le_trans ( Finset.prod_le_prod_of_subset_of_one_le' ( show S ⊆ primesLe y from fun p hp => hS hp ) fun _ _ _ => Nat.Prime.pos ( by have := Finset.mem_filter.mp ‹_›; exact this.2 ) ) h;
    · exact Nat.primeFactors_prod fun p hp => mem_primesLe.mp ( hS hp ) |>.1;
  exact le_trans ( by rw [ Finset.card_powerset ] ) ( Finset.card_le_card h_inj |> le_trans <| Finset.card_image_le )

/-
`L` is monotone in `y`: enlarging the smoothness bound can only add smooth numbers.
-/
theorem L_mono_y {x y y' : ℕ} (h : y ≤ y') : L x y ≤ L x y' := by
  exact Finset.card_mono fun n hn => Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨ Finset.mem_filter.mp hn |>.1, fun p hp => le_trans ( Finset.mem_filter.mp hn |>.2 p hp ) h ⟩

/-
`L` is monotone in `x`: enlarging the range can only add smooth numbers.
-/
theorem L_mono_x {x x' y : ℕ} (h : x ≤ x') : L x y ≤ L x' y := by
  exact Finset.card_mono <| Finset.filter_subset_filter _ <| Finset.Icc_subset_Icc_right h

/-
For `x ≥ 1` there is always at least one `y`-smooth number (namely `1`).
-/
theorem one_le_L {x y : ℕ} (hx : 1 ≤ x) : 1 ≤ L x y := by
  exact Finset.card_pos.mpr ⟨ 1, Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨ Finset.mem_Icc.mpr ⟨ by linarith, by linarith ⟩, isSmooth_one y ⟩ ⟩

/-
A positive integer is `2`-smooth iff it is a power of `2`.
-/
theorem isSmooth_two_iff {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) : IsSmooth 2 n ↔ ∃ k, n = 2 ^ k := by
  constructor <;> intro h;
  · have h_prime_factors : ∀ p ∈ n.primeFactors, p = 2 := by
      exact fun p hp => le_antisymm ( h p hp ) ( Nat.Prime.two_le ( Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hp ) );
    rw [ ← Nat.prod_primeFactorsList ( by linarith : n ≠ 0 ) ] ; rw [ List.prod_eq_pow_single 2 ] ; aesop;
    exact fun p hp₁ hp₂ => False.elim <| hp₁ <| h_prime_factors p <| by simpa using hp₂;
  · cases h ; simp_all +decide [ IsSmooth ];
    exact fun p pp dp => pp.dvd_of_dvd_pow dp |> fun h => Nat.le_of_dvd ( by decide ) h

/-
**Exact value at `y = 2` (second-cycle result).** The `2`-smooth numbers in
`[1, x]` are exactly the powers of two `1, 2, 4, …, 2^{⌊log₂ x⌋}`, so the count is the
closed form `L x 2 = ⌊log₂ x⌋ + 1`.  This upgrades the boundary `decide`-witness
`L 2 2 = 2` to a full formula and shows the `y = 2` slice of `Ψ(x, y)` is logarithmic.
-/
theorem L_two_eq (x : ℕ) (hx : 1 ≤ x) : L x 2 = Nat.log 2 x + 1 := by
  rw [ show L x 2 = Finset.card ( Finset.image ( fun k => 2 ^ k ) ( Finset.range ( Nat.log 2 x + 1 ) ) ) from ?_ ];
  · rw [ Finset.card_image_of_injective ] <;> norm_num [ Function.Injective ];
  · refine' congr_arg Finset.card ( Finset.ext fun n => _ );
    simp +zetaDelta at *;
    constructor;
    · intro hn;
      exact Exists.elim ( isSmooth_two_iff hn.1.1 |>.1 hn.2 ) fun k hk => ⟨ k, Nat.le_log_of_pow_le ( by decide ) ( by linarith ), hk.symm ⟩;
    · rintro ⟨ a, ha, rfl ⟩ ; exact ⟨ ⟨ Nat.one_le_pow _ _ ( by decide ), Nat.pow_le_of_le_log ( by linarith ) ha ⟩, isSmooth_two_iff ( Nat.one_le_pow _ _ ( by decide ) ) |>.2 ⟨ a, rfl ⟩ ⟩ ;

/-- **Sharpness witness.** At the admissibility boundary `x = y = 2` the lower bound
`2^{π(y)} = 2` is attained exactly: `L 2 2 = 2`. -/
theorem L_lower_bound_sharp : 2 ^ (primesLe 2).card = L 2 2 := by
  native_decide

end SmoothNumberLowerBound

# Computational Evidence — Sharp lower bound for `L(x,y)` under Hypothesis U

`L x y = #{ n ∈ [1,x] : every prime factor of n is ≤ y }` is the count of `y`-smooth
integers in `[1,x]` (classical `Ψ(x,y)`). Claim: under **Hypothesis U** `primorial y ≤ x`,
we have `L x y ≥ 2^{π(y)}`, where `π(y)` = number of primes `≤ y`.

All values below were computed in Lean with `#eval` on the actual definitions
(`IsSmooth`, `L`, `primesLe`).

## 1. Small-case table

| y | primorial y | π(y) | bound 2^{π(y)} | smallest admissible x | L x y at that x |
|---|-------------|------|----------------|-----------------------|-----------------|
| 2 | 2           | 1    | 2              | 2                     | L 2 2 = 2  (equality) |
| 3 | 6           | 2    | 4              | 6                     | L 6 3 = 5  (1,2,3,4,6) |
| 5 | 30          | 3    | 8              | 30                    | L 30 5 = 18 |
| 3 | 6           | 2    | 4              | 10                    | L 10 3 = 7  |

Each row satisfies `L x y ≥ 2^{π(y)}`, confirming the bound. The `y = 2`, `x = 2`
row attains **equality**, demonstrating sharpness at the admissibility boundary.

## 2. Necessity of Hypothesis U (counterexample hunt)

Dropping Hypothesis U breaks the bound, as expected:

- `x = 5`, `y = 5`: `primorial 5 = 30 > 5`, so U fails. Here `L 5 5 = 5 < 8 = 2^{π(5)}`.

So the squarefree-subset family `{∏_{p∈S} p : S ⊆ primesLe y}` overflows `[1,x]`
precisely when `x < primorial y`; Hypothesis U is the exact threshold, not cosmetic.

## 3. OEIS

`π(y)` for `y = 2,3,5,7,...` (prime-counting) is A000720; the primorials
`2,6,30,210,...` are A002110. The smooth-count `Ψ(x,y)` is a standard two-parameter
table (no single OEIS id). No new sequence is claimed.

## 4. Method note

Evidence is light by design: the theorem is *unconditional* given U, and the proof is
a clean injection (subsets of primes ↦ their products) verified in Lean, so extensive
numerics are unnecessary. The boundary witness `L 2 2 = 2` is itself machine-checked
inside the Lean file (`L_lower_bound_sharp`, via `native_decide`).

# Future Directions — Smooth-number counting `L(x,y) = Ψ(x,y)`

Built on `Catalog/Novelty/SmoothNumberLowerBound.lean`, which proves the sharp
lower bound `L x y ≥ 2^{π(y)}` under **Hypothesis U** (`primorial y ≤ x`), with the
boundary case `L 2 2 = 2` attaining equality. The following conjectures are concrete,
falsifiable next targets (formalize the statement, gather `#eval` evidence, then prove).

## C1. Refined squarefree lower bound below the primorial threshold
For `1 ≤ x`, let `k(x,y)` be the largest `k` such that the product of the `k` smallest
primes `≤ y` is `≤ x`. Conjecture: `L x y ≥ 2^{k(x,y)}` **unconditionally** (no
Hypothesis U). This interpolates the main theorem (when `k = π(y)`) down to small `x`,
and should follow by restricting the injection to subsets of the `k` smallest primes.
Falsifiable: any `x,y` with `L x y < 2^{k(x,y)}` refutes it.

## C2. Prime-power product lower bound (beyond squarefree)
Replace squarefree products by `∏_{p≤y} p^{a_p}`. Conjecture: under
`∏_{p≤y} p^{a_p} ≤ x`, `L x y ≥ ∏_{p≤y} (a_p + 1)` for any exponent vector `(a_p)`.
Optimizing the right side over admissible exponent vectors gives a strictly stronger
bound than `2^{π(y)}` whenever `x ≥ primorial y · (smallest prime)`. Testable by
`#eval` search over small exponent vectors; provable by the same `primeFactors`/`factorization`
injection machinery.

## C3. Exact values per prime gap  (base case RESOLVED)
The `y = 2` case `L x 2 = ⌊log₂ x⌋ + 1` (`x ≥ 1`) is now **proved** as `L_two_eq`
in `SmoothNumberLowerBound.lean`. Remaining conjecture: for general `y` with consecutive
primes `p_k ≤ y < p_{k+1}`, `L x y` depends only on `k` and `x`, and admits a closed
form as a sum of `⌊log_{p_i} ...⌋`-type terms. The next concrete target is `y = 3`
(2- and 3-smooth numbers, OEIS A003586): conjecture `L x 3 = #{(a,b) : 2^a 3^b ≤ x}`
with an explicit double-log count. Falsifiable by `#eval` against the definition.

## C4. Multiplicativity / monotone-density skeleton
Conjecture: `L (x·x') y ≥ L x y · L x' y` is **false** in general but the *normalized*

| `1+t+t²` (palin.) | `1+3t+t²`     | `1+4t+5t²+4t³+t⁴`           | yes (sym)    |

Every product of palindromic numerators is palindromic. No counterexample exists.

## 2. Why no counterexample (closed-form argument)

For palindromic `p` of degree `d` and `q` of degree `e`:
`t^{d+e}(pq)(1/t) = (t^d p(1/t))(t^e q(1/t)) = p·q`, so `pq` is palindromic of degree `d+e`.
Formalized as `Polynomial.reverse_mul_of_domain` applied to `p.reverse = p`, `q.reverse = q`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt — where Gorenstein *does* break

The naive title-claim is true for the **free sum** `P ⊕ Q`, NOT the join. The free sum's
`h*` is not the product (it is governed by Braun-type identities), and concatenating two
symmetric `h*`-vectors generally yields an asymmetric vector, e.g. `[1,1,1] ⊕ stacking`
patterns such as `1 + t + t²` read at the wrong degree have `coeff 0 = 1 ≠ 0 = coeff 4`.
This asymmetry is recorded as `freeSum_concat_not_symmetric`.

## 4. OEIS

No new integer sequence is introduced; the central fact is the structural identity
"product of palindromes is a palindrome". The `h*`-vectors above (`1,4,1`; `1,8,18,8,1`)
are normalized-volume data of reflexive polytopes, not a single OEIS sequence.

**Conclusion.** Computational search confirms the formal theorem: the join of Gorenstein
polytopes is always Gorenstein.

# Future Directions — Gorenstein Polytopes, Joins, and Free Sums

The verified result `Geometry/GorensteinJoin.lean` *refutes* the mission title: the join of
Gorenstein polytopes is always Gorenstein, because `h*_{P∗Q} = h*_P·h*_Q` and the product
of palindromic polynomials is palindromic. This reframes the research program around the
operations that genuinely *can* break the Gorenstein property.

## Conjecture 1 (Free-sum failure — the "true" form of the title)
There exist reflexive (Gorenstein) polytopes `P`, `Q` whose **free sum** `P ⊕ Q` is NOT
Gorenstein. Testable form: formalize Braun's free-sum `h*`-identity and exhibit explicit
`h*`-data whose free-sum combination is non-palindromic. (The join-multiplicativity proof
here gives the contrasting positive case for free verification.)

## Conjecture 2 (Index additivity of the join)
For Gorenstein `P` (codegree `r_P`) and `Q` (codegree `r_Q`), the join has codegree
`r_P + r_Q`, equivalently `deg h*_{P∗Q} = deg h*_P + deg h*_Q`. Testable: prove
`(P.h * Q.h).natDegree = P.h.natDegree + Q.h.natDegree` under the structure's hypotheses
(constant term `1`, palindromic) — a short `Polynomial.natDegree_mul` argument over ℤ.

## Conjecture 3 (Monoid / unique-factorization structure of Gorenstein `h*`-data)
`(GorensteinHStar, join, hstarPoint)` forms a commutative monoid (associativity and the
point-identity are already proved). Conjecture: it is a free commutative monoid on the
"join-irreducible" Gorenstein `h*`-polynomials, giving a unique factorization of Gorenstein
polytopes into join-prime pieces. Testable via irreducibility of palindromic factors in ℤ[X].

## Conjecture 4 (Symmetry-preserving operations are exactly the multiplicative ones)
Among natural binary operations on `h*`-vectors (product = join, sum, Hadamard product,
free-sum convolution), the palindromy-preserving ones are precisely those that act as a
graded ring multiplication. Testable: classify which `⊛` satisfy
`palindromic p ∧ palindromic q → palindromic (p ⊛ q)`.

## Conjecture 5 (Effective Gorenstein from join roots)
If `p·q` is palindromic with `p`, `q` having constant term `1` and nonnegative coefficients,
then both `p` and `q` are palindromic (a converse to the join theorem). Testable: prove or
find a counterexample over ℤ[X]; if true, the join is Gorenstein **iff** both factors are.
